### Selling the Self: Personal Branding and Impression Management on LinkedIn

### Matthew A. Gilbert

Coastal Carolina University

EXTENDED ABSTRACT

Erving Goffman’s self-presentation theory uses a theatrical metaphor to explain how people manage the impressions they make on others during social interactions. He argues that social life is like a stage performance: we are actors who craft a different persona depending on our audience. The goal is to get people to believe that their persona is authentic and that we are credible in the role we’re performing. As Goffman notes “when an individual plays a part he implicitly requests his observers to take seriously the impression that is fostered before them,” (Goffman, 1959, p. 17). Marwick & Boyd (2011) add that people present themselves differently depending on who they are talking to and where the exchange takes place. Goffman (1959) distinguishes between the front stage (where the performance happens) and the back stage (where an individual can be their true self). The theory presents the idea that social interaction involves strategic self-presentation rather than spontaneity.

Although Goffman’s theory focuses on face-to-face interactions, it can also be applied to social media (Merunková & Šlerka, 2019): the façade an individual constructs is communicated through a user’s profile and interactions. DeVito et al. (2018) note that social media users share stories and photos that affect how others perceive them. Goffman (1959) refers to this as impression management. This digital landscape for impression management is vast. According to Rivera (2025), approximately 5.52 billion people worldwide used the internet (67.5% of the population), with 5.22 billion active on social media. In the United States, YouTube (84% of the population) and Facebook (71% of the population) are the most widely used platforms (Gottfried & Park, 2025). Forty-three percent of social media users have a profile on LinkedIn, which equates to more than 1 billion members (Sprout Social, 2025).

LinkedIn differs from other social media networks because its purpose is personal promotion and professional networking (Utz & Breuer, 2019). It is an ideal platform to research how individuals present their idealized self on the front stage to colleagues and others in industry. Given its professional context, the performance of self on LinkedIn aligns with personal branding. Traditional branding is the process by which products are marketed as unique and distinctive; the term became associated with marketing individuals in the 1990s (Brems et al., 2017). Peters (1997; 1999) is credited with coining the term “personal branding” to represent the process of marketing people. As explained by Brems et al. (2017) “personal branding is... a matter of knowing your skills and persona, and presenting them on a well-arranged platter to others” (p. 445).

Drawing on self-presentation theory, this study explores how individuals on LinkedIn perform identity to position themselves as professionals and, to a large degree, products in a digital

marketplace that rewards visibility and engagement. Users leverage self-presentation strategies to build personal brands in an online environment shaped by the economics of attention. Professionals balance sincerity with strategy by presenting themselves as authentic while optimizing their visibility and credibility to achieve career goals. This research examines how professionals manage identity, communicate authenticity, construct credibility, and deploy narratives to build their brands through different content formats and engagement tactics.

Using qualitative content analysis, this study examines publicly available LinkedIn posts from 50 professionals in five occupational categories(10 individuals per category): marketing and branding specialists; entrepreneurs and founders; educators and coaches; corporate managers and executives; career advisors and recruiters. These categories were selected to capture diverse professional contexts and varied approaches to self-presentation. Participants with a minimum of 1,000 connections who post at least once a week will be selected through purposive sampling. Five posts per participant will be analyzed for a total of 250 posts, collected over a two-month period to capture consistency in self-presentation strategies. Posts will be selected to represent different content types (text-only, image-based, video, article shares, and carousel posts) to examine how self-presentation varies across formats.

The analysis will use deductive coding guided by Goffman’s concepts of front-stage performance and impression management. Specific coding categories will include visual self-presentation elements (profile photos, background images, multimedia content), linguistic strategies (tone, vocabulary, use of first-person narrative), content themes (professional achievements, thought leadership, vulnerability displays), and engagement tactics (calls to action, question prompts, storytelling techniques). To protect participant privacy, identifying information such as names, company affiliations, and distinctive biographical details will be anonymized in reporting findings.

NVivo software in conjunction with the NCapture browser extension will be used to systematically organize and analyze the data. The software allows researchers to organize and code multiple data sources, assign attributes for comparison, add interpretations, query data, and create visualizations (Swygart-Hobaugh, 2025). Lumivero (2023) shares that NVivo is frequently used for qualitative data analysis. Swygart-Hobaugh (2025) adds that researchers should “use NVivo software for qualitative analysis of textual and audiovisual data sources” (para. 1).

This study contributes to marketing theory and practice by conceptualizing personal branding as both a communication practice and an economic behavior. By integrating perspectives from marketing and sociology, the study addresses a gap in understanding how professionals strategically navigate identity construction on career-focused platforms. The research illuminates how digital professionals balance the demands of authenticity, visibility, and strategic positioning within systems that transform personal identity into professional capital.

Keywords: digital identity, Erving Goffman, front-stage performance, impression management, LinkedIn, personal branding, professional identity, qualitative content analysis, self-presentation theory, social media marketing

References are available upon request.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Matthew A. Gilbert (MBA, Woodbury University) is a teacher, researcher, and trainer with more than 25 years of experience consulting, speaking, and writing. A lecturer of marketing at Coastal Carolina University, he teaches advertising, personal selling, and principles of marketing. His research investigates how artificial intelligence, marketing technology, and social media transform learning, communication, and consumer engagement. He also explores marketing strategies in sports and innovation in entrepreneurship education. Beyond his research, he develops training workshops, consults on communication and curriculum, and has delivered three TEDx Talks. He is the author of Kickstarting Your Marketing, a principles of marketing textbook, and has published book chapters examining AI applications in marketing, global sports marketing strategies, and entrepreneurship education.

## Abstract
The notion of self-branding has drawn myriad academic responses over the last decade. First popularised in a provocative piece published in Fast Company, self-branding has been criticised by some on theoretical, practical and ethical grounds, while others have endorsed and propelled the idea. This article considers how and why the concept of self-branding has become so prevalent. We contend that it parallels the growth of digital technology (particularly social media) embedded in the current political climate: neoliberal individualism. Another objective here is to imbue the concept of self-branding with a marketing perspective and show how the ‘celebrities’ of self-branding manifest at a marketing media nexus distinct to the opening decades of the twenty-first century. Building on literature from mostly media and cultural studies, this critique sees self-branding as a distortion of key branding principles that has obvious implications for its practitioners and advocates. The article shows that, despite inherent tensions and problematic ironies, self-branding persists through the rise of Social Media Influencers; we consider three of these whose fame and following was achieved via the practices and phenomena under consideration.

Introduction
Self-branding, which is sometimes called personal branding, involves individuals devel-
oping a distinctive public image for commercial gain and/or cultural capital. The number
of books, websites, workshops and seminars devoted to its principles and promotion is
evidence of its prevalence and appeal (Khedher2014, p. 30). Central to self-branding is
the idea that, just like commercially branded products, individuals beneﬁt from having a
unique selling point, or a public identity that is singularly charismatic and responsive to
the needs and interests of target audiences. This idea has permeated business literature
since at least the 1920s, with best-selling titles that extol the merits of self-improvement
and a positive attitude, but its broader resonance over the last 20 years is signiﬁcant. In
terms of pushing the idea of self-branding from the margins of marketing literature to
the forefront of mainstream media, a 1997 article published in the business magazine

Fast Companybears noting. In the article‘The Brand Called You’, Tom Peters argues that
individuals must assume control of their own brand identity to stand out in the labour
market, project a dynamic and memorable image, and consistently deliver value to
consumers, employers and markets. Grafting the logic of branding onto individuals is
not only possible or desirable, he argues; it is imperative and inevitable.
Lest individuals surrender their brand identities to others, for lack of initiative, interest
or strategy, Peters believes that self-branding requires the same dedication and drive
that saw the likes of Nike and Starbucks achieve prominence and loyalty. He writes:‘We
are CEOs of our own companies: Me Inc. To be in business today, our most important job
is to be head marketer of the brand called You’(Peters1997). Peters thus encourages
individuals to turn their résumé into a‘marketing brochure’full of‘braggables’for which
they want to be famous (the term he uses):‘being CEO of Me Inc. requires you to act
selﬁshly–to grow yourself, to promote yourself, to get the market to reward yourself’
(Peters1997). His message captured popular audiences with its clarity, simplicity and
conviction; and, as argued shortly, its seamless consonance with the reigning tenets of a
neoliberal ideology.
A problematic concept and practice
Branding is inextricably tied to marketing; however, the concept of self-branding does
notﬁt neatly as a subset of branding, and scaling the branding concept down to the
individual is problematic. Branding an individual raises conceptual, practical and ethical
issues, which are either not acknowledged or are simply glossed over by its advocates.
Moreover, there is an implicit assumption that everyone is expected to self-brand in
order to realise his or her fullest potential. There is even a call for academics to build a
personal brand in order to help sell their university online (Brandabur2012), while one
researcher has developed (albeit facetiously) the‘Kardashian Index’to measure the
popularity of scientists by their number of followers on Twitter (Hall2014).
The word‘brand’is derived from the Old Norse wordbrandr, meaning‘to burn’, and
referred to the practice whereby livestock owners would burn a unique and diﬀerentiat-
ing symbol into their animals’skins. In its contemporary use for marketing, a brand
signiﬁes a certain quality or idea associated with a commodity which ostensibly simpli-
ﬁes the consumer’s decision-making. Ideally, a brand must be seen to possess strong,
favourable, unique and relevant mental associations (Keller2007), which helps diﬀer-
entiate the brand in an otherwise crowded and cacophonous market. Another function
of branding is to imbue the product, service orﬁrm with a personality. Presumably,
personality dimensions such as ruggedness, sophistication, sincerity, excitement and
competence (Aaker1997) give a product, service orﬁrm a human-like quality and thus
make it more relatable. The brand’s usefulness therefore rests on the promise of
consistency, which mitigates risks for the consumer. That is, one can more or less
know what to expect when they commit to a reputable brand: the Starbucks‘experi-
ence’varies little from Sydney to New York to Shanghai, and this holds more or less true
for Nike, Apple, Coke and so on. The brand’s consistency thus encourages repeat
purchases (over space and time) and, most importantly, brand loyalty.
Herein lays the obvious problem when the concept of branding is applied to a
person: consistency is notoriously diﬃcult to sustain. One needs only to consider the

when they deviate from policies and are then punished by voters for having abandoned

Despite these issues, the concept of self-branding continues to be both popular and
inﬂuential. However apart from the issue of maintaining consistency (and hence authen-
ticity), the‘ordinary’person wanting to be famous faces another major hurdle: how to
build and cultivate a large target audience. To make sense of this, we need to consider
the interplay between marketing, media and celebrity.
Audience size and celebrity: where does the opportunity lie?
Marketing and media are mutually dependent. Media relies on advertising revenue for
commercial viability, while advertisers have traditionally relied on media to address the
audience (their potential consumers). To deliver an audience, media organisations create
interesting, engaging content; this is their primary objective. One type of content that
has been broadly popular with audiences is celebrity.
There is an obvious marketing relationship between a brand, media, audience and
celebrity. At a basic level, the brand represents the identity of a commodity (a product,
service orﬁrm), and its main function is to convey a certain level of quality. But to reach
the target audience (at an optimal frequency) with its message, the brand owners (or
advertisers) have to pay media organisations for the advertising. When a celebrity, or a
human brand, is introduced into the picture, the dynamics change slightly. A human
brand is deﬁned here as‘any well-known persona who is the subject of marketing
communications eﬀorts’(Thomson2006, p. 104). The biggest change is that the human
brand can now bring his or her own audience into the equation. Of course, the human
brand can still rely on traditional media to deliver the audience. But celebrities with a
following can also use their own media (e.g. websites, blogs, Facebook, Twitter and
Instagram) to inﬂuence this audience (e.g. the Kardashians). Eventually, with consistent
juxtaposition, the human brand can become synonymous with the brand and hence
with the product, service orﬁrm. This suggests that self-branding makes most sense if
celebrities can lend their names proﬁtably to major brands. Sports stars, for instance, can
earn many times more from their endorsement fees than from prize money. This is
because major sporting events command a large audience. This provides the endorsed

The opportunity may lie in social media (and/or reality television) to help build a strong

we now return to our original question of why self-branding has continued to grow in
popularity. We contend that there are three main reasons for the rise of self-branding:
(1) Social media tacitlypromises fame (and subsequent wealth) to‘ordinary’users
and thus encourages practices of micro-celebrity.
(2)Within a political culture of neoliberal individualism, self-branding is encouraged
with the promise of reward.
(3)The commercial viability of some Social Media Inﬂuencers (SMIs; to be discussed
shortly), whose success depends on self-branding and practices of micro-celebrity,
has proven to be both inspirational and seemingly replicable.
Our contention is that the increased ease of projecting one’s image through social
media coupled with the rise of individualism has made the notion of self-branding more
popular. This in turn creates the illusion–often exempliﬁed by the success of reality
television stars–that anyone can be famous and hence become ostensibly successful.
Social media and the practices of micro-celebrity
Peters (1997) did not attribute the importance of self-branding exclusively to the
Internet, but his central message has certainly been ampliﬁed and extended by others
who see in the digital age a heightened need for the practices and mind-set that Peters

Self-branding operates through principles and practices distinct to the‘promotional
culture’(Wernick1992) of advanced consumer capitalism. It shows how private indivi-

thus represents a seminal turning point in how subjectivity itself is understood and

political upheaval, and the concept of self-branding manifests as an apposite naviga-

through social media can be understood as a way to retain and assert personal agency

with neoliberal notions of individual eﬃcacy and responsibility; and rests on capitalist

Recent cases of self-branding and the rise of social media inﬂuencers
To consider strategies of micro-celebrity in practice, and to see the phenomena dis-
cussed thus far manifest with varying consequences, three recent examples are highly
pertinent. These examples illustrate a particular kind of online micro-celebrity: the SMI.
As Hearn and Schoenhoﬀexplain:‘The SMI works to generate a form of“celebrity”
capital by cultivating as much attention as possible and crafting an authentic“personal
brand”via social networks, which can subsequently be used by companies and adver-
tisers for consumer outreach’(2016, p. 194). SMIs determine their success in terms of
return on inﬂuence as marketers seek them out to capitalise on their wide social
networks and beneﬁt from the intimate, more‘trustworthy’relationships SMIs have
ostensibly created (2016, p. 203, Gormley2016).
In 2015, two Australian food bloggers made headlines for very diﬀerent but not
entirely unrelated reasons. In February, Jess Anscough–better known to her fans as the
Wellness Warrior–died from a rare form of cancer, epithelioid sarcoma, at the age of 30.
Anscough, who had been diagnosed seven years earlier, and had lost her mother Sharyn
to breast cancer in 2013, found social media fame by eschewing conventional cancer
treatment and instead advocating the controversial Gerson Therapy (Corderoy2015).
Developed in the 1930s, Gerson Therapy claims to cure cancer and other degenerative
diseases through diet, which for Anscough entailed huge amounts of fruit and vegeta-
bles and up to six daily coﬀee enemas. In April, 23-year-old Belle Gibson, who found
social media fame by claiming to have cured her terminal brain cancer through diet and
lifestyle alone, revealed that she had lied about having cancer (Davey2015, Phillip2015).
By the time her hoax was exposed, Gibson’s empire, under the name‘The Whole Pantry’,
had grown from a blog to a widely publicised phone app and a book deal. This article is
not concerned so much with the ire, scepticism or pity these women generated in their
eager embrace of‘wellness’strategies that were obviously contentious: their fame
rested on their rejection of conventional medicine and science. Instead, it is argued
here that, by strategically embedding compelling narratives within their respective
online personas, both Anscough and Gibson show how contemporary social media
enables and powers online celebrity, whereby‘ordinary’users cultivate fame and inﬂu-
ence that can be then leveraged more widely.
Through stories that were inspirational, accessible and consistent with burgeoning
mainstream interest in‘wellness’, the process of making active choices towards a healthy
and fulﬁlling life, Anscough and Gibson attracted fan bases, media attention and cultural
traction. Both had also traded on one of the most import facets of micro-celebrity: a
promise of‘authenticity’. Micro-celebrity is a mind-set and a set of practices that courts
attention through insights into its practitioners’private lives, and a sense of realness that
renders their narratives, their branding, both accessible and intimate. That is, writes

in April 2011 and chronicled how she regained her health and vitality after an appen-

understand the typical American food system. Aghast at what she considered an alarm-

the‘truth’behind packaged, processed foods and to lobby for greater transparency on

over 46,000 followers and her Twitter handle had over 89,000 followers.

found both fame and marketability through strategic self-branding. Ultimately (and
obviously) Hari, aka the Food Babe, has been the most successful. As James Hamblin
(2015) wrote inThe Atlantic, hyperbolically perhaps,‘the idea of a lone consultant
becoming, in three short years, more inﬂuential than entire university departments of
Ph.Ds., is indicative of a new level of potential for celebrity in health messaging’. That is
not to say that her contribution to the wellness industry has been any more robust,
considered or valid–on social media, celebrity is not necessarily dependent on such
‘logical’indices. Hari has been the subject of much derision from science writers
precisely because of her populist spin on nutritional advice, but her proﬁle continues
to grow, with coverage across theNew York Times, NBC News and theWashington Post
and her appointment as CNN’s food expert. She is a savvy entrepreneur as much as a
consumer advocate, and sells eating guides with meal calendars, recipes and grocery
lists replete with‘approved brands’–that is, those with which she has a commercial
arrangement (Schultz and Morrison2014). The size of her fan base bodes well for her

including Subway, Lean Cuisine, McDonalds, General Mills, Starbucks and Coca-Cola–all

what she claimed were harmful chemicals in their foods. The Food Babe’s brand is
strong, distinctive and consistent, much to the chagrin of actual scientists who argue
that just because an ingredient is hard to pronounce or is indecipherable for the average
consumer this does not render it dangerous (Gorski2014). Moreover, like Anscough and
Gibson, she has a story–a journey to‘wellness’through diet–that has been reconﬁ-
gured as a popularly accessible promise.
Conclusion
The aim of this article is to critically examine the idea of self-brandingﬁrst popularised in the
1990s. Although it is conceptuallyﬂawed, its popularity has not waned. The question is
why? In terms of the examples considered (Anscough, Gibson and Hari), the issue is not their
motivations, credentials or even sincerity. Rather, it is the degree to which contemporary
social, economic and technological processes both accommodate and reward their style of
message management, insofar as social media propelled them from relative obscurity to

become prominent SMIs, and the role of self-branding in this development. Their visibility
and eﬃcacy are clearly indebted to communication capabilities distinct to the early twenty-
ﬁrst century, and a cultural milieu increasingly primed for self-promotion and triumphant
individualism. This article shows how social media encourages the practices of self-branding
that these three women engaged in. At stake is how these practices capitalise on the
apparent democratisation of media production and distribution, whereby entry levelsare
comparatively low and potential reach, in terms of audience and inﬂuence, is spectacularly
high. The wide-ranging eﬀects of participatory media and user-generated content have
been amply documented and discussed for almost two decades. It is argued here, however,
that, in the early twenty-ﬁrst century, key trends appear especially pronounced–not the
least of which is the extent to which socialmedia like Facebook, Twitter, YouTube and
Instagram facilitate not just participation but practices of self-branding.
The rapid globalisation of advanced consumer capitalism has obviously widened the
scope and scale of all brand marketing, but it is the ascent and entrenchment of self-
branding that is considered here, and the ways this phenomenon links dominant
notions of individual success, personal responsibility and subjectivity to a political
economy deﬁned almost completely by consumerist logic. Our analysis suggests that
the rise of social media and our current consumerist orientation may have contributed
to this popularity. The rise of both‘Instafame’and SMIs–their pursuit and realisation–
eﬀectively underscores three distinct and interrelated processes: the transformative and
seminal eﬀects of social, interactive and conversational media in the Information Age;
the mercurial dismantling of what were once‘knowledge monopolies’, as the likes of
Anscough, Gibson and Hari become quasi-experts and assume the role historically
reserved for highly trained specialists (such as doctors, dieticians and scientists); and
the near-total extension of marketing logic and language into more areas of contem-
porary social life. While all these processes predate and are not exclusive to social media,
cumulatively social media intensiﬁes and spotlights their salience.

Purpose
YouTube, a popular source for diverse information, hosts a wealth of content on aesthetic canthoplasty. Yet, concerns linger about the accuracy and reliability of these videos, with potential for inaccuracies, biases, or misleading information. This study aims to evaluate the quality and reliability of YouTube content on this sought-after facial enhancement procedure.
Methods
The study employs four distinct scoring tools: the Global Quality Score (GQS), the Medical Quality Video Evaluation Tool (MQ-VET), the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Audiovisual Materials (PEMAT-A/V), and the Video Power Index (VPI).
Results
Analysis of a total of 173 YouTube videos relevant to aesthetic canthoplasty revealed scores that were primarily indicative of poor quality and reliability.(Mean score ±SD, PEMAT A/V: 30.75 ±28.8, MQ-VET: 28.57 ±12.6, GQS: 1.7 ±1) Notably, these videos were predominantly uploaded by healthcare professionals (82.1%), and they focused more on advertisements (46.2%) than on scientific or educational information. Their elevated viewership and engagement metrics (likes, comments, and shares) attest to their significant popularity and influence. (Mean VPI score: 176.6 ±635.8).
Conclusion
YouTube’s influence on aesthetic eyelid surgery is undeniable, shaping patient choices and expectations. However, unrealistic beauty ideals, heightened body dissatisfaction, and social comparisons lurk within its content, potentially harming psychological well-being and surgical decisions. Prioritizing qualified medical guidance and critical evaluation of online information are crucial for patients. Authors and platforms must act responsibly: authors by producing high-quality content, platforms by tackling misinformation.

Diffused audiences sometimes, through their engagement with social media, connect with micro-celebrities in order to make sense of their world. results.snippet:
The findings show that social media content significantly influences perceptions of professional competence and person–organization fit, thereby altering hiring intention. In particular, negative social media content was found to overshadow the professional competence signal, even for highly qualified candidates, leading to a prioritization of perceived cultural fit. In contrast, professional content enabled candidates to send a positive fit signal, supporting hiring intention.

## Summary
Across the provided scholarly sources, “personal branding” in online contexts is framed as strategic self-presentation designed to signal identity, competence, and credibility, often drawing from microcelebrity practices that cultivate affective ties with niche audiences. Core themes include: (1) microcelebrity and self-branding as intertwined practices; (2) impression management tactics on professional networks (e.g., LinkedIn); (3) perceived authenticity achieved through curated intimacy; and (4) credibility concerns in “Instafamous” influencer contexts. The sources are largely conceptual or qualitative; none report causal effect sizes or quantified performance lifts. The set provides little or no empirical evidence on: entrepreneur/senior-leader visibility effects on organizational outcomes, or measured differences between individual and organizational accounts. Where marketing or vendor literatures commonly claim numerical “authenticity” or “CEO visibility” performance boosts, those statistics are not substantiated in these sources.

## Key Findings
- Microcelebrity: definition and core practices
  - Microcelebrity is being well known to a niche audience and involves presenting oneself as a public persona, building affective ties, and treating followers as fans; it is tightly linked to self-branding online [1]. The sources describe practices and logics but do not report numerical effect sizes [1].

- Self-branding as entrepreneurial labor and commodification of the self
  - Self-branding and micro-celebrity are co-constitutive; influencers monetize identity and image, crafting “intimate” exchanges that audiences read as authentic. This is documented as a socio-cultural shift rather than quantified performance change [5], [7]. No numerical effect sizes are reported in these sources [5], [7].

- Perceived authenticity via “intimate exchange” and backstage access
  - Influencers’ profiles give followers access to what appears to be “genuine, raw” aspects of life; this “perceived authenticity” is cultivated and monetized through self-branding practices [7]. The source emphasizes perception and craft rather than measured authenticity indices; no effect sizes are reported [7].

- Credibility and self-presentation of “Instafamous” micro-celebrities
  - Firms increasingly use micro-celebrities for endorsements while credibility concerns persist. Credibility is tied to self-presentation choices and perceived authenticity in followers’ eyes [8]. The cited work focuses on credibility themes; it does not provide quantitative endorsement effectiveness or effect sizes in this set [8].

- “#NoFilter” and authenticity signaling on Instagram
  - Micro-celebrities deploy self-branding practices that specifically perform authenticity (e.g., aesthetic and textual cues such as “no filter”). The study situates these tactics within classic impression management/presentation-of-self frameworks, but the provided material does not report numerical engagement lifts or causal effects [2].

- Conceptual foundations: presentation of self and online personal branding processes
  - The literature anchors in Goffman’s presentation-of-self and related impression management concepts, adapted to platform logics. Online personal branding is positioned as the strategic management of identity signals to convey professional value, credibility, and competence [2], [3]. These sources outline processes rather than reporting quantitative outcomes [2], [3].

- Impression management on LinkedIn
  - LinkedIn personal branding relies on recognizable impression management tactics (e.g., curated profiles, strategic self-promotion, endorsements), adapted to a professional context. The proceedings paper synthesizes these practices conceptually; no numeric effect sizes or hiring/engagement lifts are reported in the provided excerpt [4].

- Microcelebrity and the branded self: frameworks and historical development
  - The “branded self” framework links everyday self-presentation to market logics under social media conditions, offering a conceptual map for how individuals narrate identity as brand assets [6]. This source is theoretical; it does not report empirical effect sizes [6].

- Parasocial dynamics and relationship-building
  - Across the microcelebrity literature here, audience connections are described as affective and intimate—resembling fan relationships—which underpin engagement and perceived authenticity [1], [7]. The sources describe these ties conceptually; no quantified strength-of-relationship or causal engagement metrics are provided [1], [7].

- Entrepreneur/senior-leader visibility effects on organizational outcomes
  - Not covered: None of the provided sources present empirical tests or effect sizes linking leader visibility on social media to organizational performance outcomes. This remains a gap in this source set.

- Measured differences between individual and organizational accounts
  - Not covered: The sources do not provide comparative, quantitative analyses of how individual versus organizational accounts differ in reach, engagement, trust, or other outcomes.

## Evidence Quality
- Study types and rigor
  - Peer-reviewed journal articles with qualitative/interpretive or conceptual emphases: [2], [5], [7], [8].
  - Scholarly overviews/conceptual chapters or essays: [1], [3], [6].
  - Conference proceedings (scholarly but not a peer-reviewed journal article): [4].
  - Across the set, most evidence is conceptual or qualitative; there are no randomized experiments, quasi-experiments, or panel econometric analyses reporting effect sizes on outcomes like engagement rates, hiring decisions, sales, or firm performance.

- Consensus vs. contested points
  - Broad consensus:
    - Self-branding and microcelebrity involve strategic self-presentation aimed at cultivating affective ties and perceived authenticity [1], [5], [7].
    - Authenticity is frequently “performed” or curated, not simply spontaneous [2], [7].
    - Credibility is bound up with self-presentation choices and audience perceptions [8].
  - Tensions (preserved rather than resolved):
    - Authenticity as sincere expression versus as performed strategy: Sources emphasize curation/performance (e.g., “perceived authenticity,” backstage access as tactic) [2], [7], while also noting audiences experience these exchanges as intimate and genuine [7]. The set does not adjudicate this tension empirically with effect sizes.
    - Commercialization vs. community: The literature profiles both monetization and community/affective ties, but does not quantify trade-offs [5], [7], [1].

- Absent or unverified statistics
  - The provided sources do not report quantitative “lift” statistics (e.g., “authentic posts raise engagement by X%,” “CEO visibility increases firm performance by Y%”) or primary-effect sizes on hiring outcomes from LinkedIn profile tactics. Any such widely repeated vendor or agency numbers are not evidenced in this set.

## Open Questions
- Causal effects and magnitudes
  - What are the causal effects (and effect sizes) of specific self-branding tactics (e.g., authenticity signals like “#NoFilter,” backstage content) on measurable outcomes (engagement, conversions, employability)? Not addressed with quantitative evidence in these sources [2], [3], [7], [8].
- Leadership visibility and organizational performance
  - Do entrepreneur/senior-leader posts measurably affect firm-level outcomes (revenue growth, recruiting efficiency, valuation)? No evidence in this set; rigorous causal identification remains an open need.
- Comparative analyses: individual vs. organizational accounts
  - How do audiences differentially evaluate credibility, authenticity, and trust across personal versus corporate accounts, and with what effect sizes on behavior? Not covered here.
- Boundary conditions and heterogeneity
  - How do platform affordances, industry, gender, and cultural context moderate the relationship between self-presentation, perceived authenticity, and outcomes? The set notes context and culture conceptually but provides no quantitative moderation analyses [5], [7], [8].
- Measurement of parasocial ties in professional networks
  - How can parasocial or affective ties be validly measured on professional platforms like LinkedIn, and how do they relate to hiring decisions and reputation? Not quantified in this set [1], [4], [7].
